title: How to Use Social Media Without Losing Your Soul
author: Kathleen Abela
summary: In this interview, Kathleen Abela talks with Adele Collins — a Harvard-educated mother of eight and the creator of the Instagram account @Simplelifemusings — about how she has used social media as a mother without letting it hollow out her interior life. Collins traces her account's evolution from a simple, haiku-like way of staying in touch with family after an unplanned cross-country move, into a platform for sharing a Catholic vision of family culture and the dignity of motherhood. Her central argument is that social media metrics are a poor proxy for value: a post can go viral 'but that does not mean that they are valuable things that have contributed to somebody's formation,' and she instead judges her own content by whether it builds community, teaches something, or merely courts algorithm-friendly controversy. She is candid about the mechanics of monetization for those who choose it, but describes her own current use as intentionally small — a 'hobby' of one to three posts a week, notifications off, with no goal of growing her 57,000-follower account. Throughout, she frames a coherent 'higher purpose' — helping women see motherhood as beautiful rather than merely chaotic — as the discipline that keeps her from being captured by the platform's gamified incentives.

quotes: I think that gamifying things works really well for human psychology. There’s something about us that we just love to see the challenge of something, and all social media has definitely used that to its advantage.
Regarding the metrics, they can tell you how many people have seen a post. They don’t tell you if that post was worth seeing.
Things will go viral, but that does not mean that they are valuable things that have contributed to somebody’s formation. That’s where sometimes the algorithm is at odds with what our work is.

From the very beginning of Instagram, I always had my notifications turned off on my phone. Otherwise, notifications are constantly popping up: so-and-so liked it, or commented. I don’t want to have that following me everywhere.

I’m more interested in the best things that have come from Instagram, which have actually happened off Instagram. I’m interested in human connections, and that’s a very different goal than if you’re trying to grow an account or if you’re trying to increase your reach or all of those things.
It’s not degrading to who you are to be a mother. It’s not a second choice or a fallback or a failure. This is a real pinnacle of womanhood. Being a mother is really beautiful.

A much better question is: was this thing something that was encouraging a conversation and building a community? Was it contributing to formation? Was it teaching something, or was it just creating controversy?
